# Phylogenetics: Crabs and a Campus Outbreak

In this lab you'll use phylogenetic trees for two things real scientists do with them:

1. **Catch a fungus.** A zombie-ant-style fungus (*Ophiocordyceps*) is infecting students in two dorms. You have DNA from the patients and from three suspects. You'll build a tree to figure out where the outbreak came from, who infected whom, and whether the mycology lab is to blame. This is called **genomic epidemiology**, and it's the same approach public health labs used to track SARS-CoV-2, mpox and *Candida auris* outbreaks.

2. **Is everything turning into a crab?** The internet jokes that every animal eventually evolves into a crab. It's actually half true! You'll use **ancestral state reconstruction** to find out how many times evolution "invented" the crab body, and whether it ever un-invented it.

in R:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(ape)
library(phangorn)
library(phytools)
```


## Part 1: The Campus Outbreak

### The case

> **URGENT – Office of the Dean of Students**
>
> Over the past three weeks, 16 students from **Dorm A** and **Dorm B** have come to Health Services with fatigue, an unusual craving to climb to high places, and a fuzzy white growth behind the ears. Culture results show an *Ophiocordyceps* fungus.
>
> We have sequenced the same 1.5 kb marker gene from every patient, and from three possible sources:
>
> - **`Forest_*`**: wild *Ophiocordyceps* collected in the woods behind campus.
> - **`LabStock_*`**: strains from the mycology lab's freezer. (The mycology lab says it's definitely not them.)
> - **`Smoothie_*`**: fungus cultured from two lots of "Brain Boost" mushroom powder sold at the campus smoothie bar.
>
> A *Cordyceps militaris* sequence is included as an outgroup.
>
> We need to know: **Where did this come from? Is it spreading between dorms? Who is to blame?**

### Introduction to `IQ-tree`

For this part, you'll build the tree yourself. We will use [`IQ-tree`](http://www.iqtree.org/), one of the most widely used programs for building phylogenetic trees. `IQ-tree`:

- Uses **maximum likelihood**: it searches for the tree that makes your data most probable under a model of evolution.
- Runs **ModelFinder** first to pick the best model of substitution for your data (remember AIC/BIC from lecture).
- Runs **ultrafast bootstraps** to tell you how much to trust each branch. Bootstrap values above 75% are generally considered well supported, and above 95% strongly supported.

The basic command, run from the **Terminal**, is:

```
iqtree2 -s your_alignment.fasta -B 1000
```

> **Tip:** `IQ-tree` won't overwrite an earlier run with the same name. If you need to rerun something, add `-redo` to the command.

9. Download `outbreak_unaligned.fasta` and `outbreak_metadata.csv` from Moodle and put them in your `~/phylo_lab` folder.

### Align the sequences

10. These sequences have insertions and deletions, so they need aligning first. Align them with `MAFFT`:

```
system('mafft --auto outbreak_unaligned.fasta > outbreak_aligned.fasta')
```

11. Build the tree:

```
system('iqtree2 -s outbreak_aligned.fasta -B 1000 --prefix outbreak')
```

12. Plot it in R, coloring the samples by where they came from:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
meta <- read.csv("outbreak_metadata.csv")
tr   <- read.tree("outbreak.treefile")
tr   <- root(tr, outgroup = "Outgroup_Cordyceps", resolve.root = TRUE)

colors <- c("Forest" = "darkgreen", "LabStock" = "purple", "Smoothie" = "orange",
            "Infected student" = "red", "Outgroup (C. militaris)" = "grey40")
tip_source <- meta$source[match(tr$tip.label, meta$sample)]

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plot(tr, tip.color = colors[tip_source], cex = 0.8)
nodelabels(tr$node.label, frame = "none", adj = c(1.2, -0.4), cex = 0.6)
add.scale.bar()
legend("right", legend = names(colors), text.col = colors, bty = "n")
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Question 8

- Something is very wrong with one sample. Which one, and what about the tree tells you so? Open `outbreak_aligned.fasta` in the [NCBI MSA viewer](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/msaviewer/) (use `Coloring -> Nucleic Acid Colors`) to look at that sample. What do you see?
```

### Fix it

13. Somebody in the sequencing facility loaded one sample backwards: it's the **reverse complement** of the real sequence. `MAFFT` can detect and flip backwards sequences for you:

```
system('mafft --adjustdirectionaccurately --auto outbreak_unaligned.fasta > outbreak_fixed.fasta')
system('iqtree2 -s outbreak_fixed.fasta -B 1000 --prefix outbreak_fixed')
```

`MAFFT` adds `_R_` to the start of the name of any sequence it flipped. Run `grep "_R_" outbreak_fixed.fasta` to check which one it was. Then clean up the name in R before plotting, and replot your tree using `outbreak_fixed.treefile`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tr <- read.tree("outbreak_fixed.treefile")
tr$tip.label <- sub("^_R_", "", tr$tip.label)
# ...then root and plot exactly as in step 12
```

### Solve the case

14. Now color the infected students by **dorm** instead of by source:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
tip_dorm <- meta$dorm[match(tr$tip.label, meta$sample)]
dorm_colors <- ifelse(is.na(tip_dorm), "grey60",
                      ifelse(tip_dorm == "Dorm_A", "blue", "red"))
plot(tr, tip.color = dorm_colors, cex = 0.8)
nodelabels(tr$node.label, frame = "none", adj = c(1.2, -0.4), cex = 0.6)
legend("right", legend = c("Dorm A", "Dorm B", "Not a patient"),
       text.col = c("blue", "red", "grey60"), bty = "n")
```

15. Use code to check your hypotheses. `is.monophyletic()` tells you whether a group of samples forms a single clade with nothing else mixed in:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
patients <- grep("Patient", tr$tip.label, value = TRUE)
is.monophyletic(tr, patients)
is.monophyletic(tr, c(patients, "Smoothie_LotA", "Smoothie_LotB"))
is.monophyletic(tr, c(patients, "LabStock_1", "LabStock_2", "LabStock_3"))
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 9 - 12

- Is this a single outbreak (one introduction) or several separate infections from the environment? How do you know?
- Which suspect is the source: the forest, the lab or the smoothie bar? Which node in the tree supports your answer, and what is its bootstrap value?
- The mycology lab strains are not the source, but they are fairly closely related to the outbreak. Why might someone who looked at the tree too quickly have blamed the lab?
- Are there separate transmission clusters for each dorm? One student's tree position doesn't match their dorm. Who is it, and what could explain it? (Think about how students from different dorms might come into contact.)
```

## Part 2: Is Everything Turning Into a Crab?

### Carcinization

In 1916 the zoologist L.A. Borradaile noticed that unrelated crustaceans kept evolving into crab-shaped animals, and called it *"one of the many attempts of Nature to evolve a crab."* The process now has a name: **carcinization**.

Here's the twist: not every crab is a crab.

- **True crabs (Brachyura):** blue crabs, edible crabs, spider crabs, ghost crabs...
- **False crabs (Anomura):** the relatives of hermit crabs and squat lobsters. Some of them (king crabs, porcelain crabs) look *exactly* like crabs, but evolved that shape on their own.

Evolution can also go the other way: some crab-shaped lineages *lost* the crab body. That's called **decarcinization**.

In this lab, an animal counts as **crab-like** if it has **both** of these:

1. a wide, flat, hard upper shell (the carapace), and
2. the abdomen (the "tail") folded tightly underneath the body.

A hermit crab has a soft abdomen curled into a snail shell, so it's not crab-like. A lobster has a long tail sticking out the back, so it's not crab-like either.

**Ancestral state reconstruction (ASR)** takes a tree and the traits we can see in living species, and estimates what the traits were in ancestors we can't see. That lets us count how many times a trait was gained or lost.

### The data

We'll use 36 decapod crustaceans. The tree is a simplified version of published phylogenies of crabs and their relatives (Bracken-Grissom et al. 2013, *BMC Evolutionary Biology*; Wolfe et al. 2021, *BioEssays*). Some relationships are still debated, so where the experts don't agree, the tree has a **polytomy** (a node with more than two branches).

1. Load the tree and the trait data:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
decapods <- read.tree(text = "((Homarus_americanus,Procambarus_clarkii),((Dromia_personata,(Homola_barbata,(Ranina_ranina,((Callinectes_sapidus,Cancer_pagurus,Macrocheira_kaempferi,Carcinus_maenas,Menippe_mercenaria),(Ocypode_quadrata,Leptuca_pugilator,Grapsus_grapsus))))),((Emerita_analoga,Emerita_talpoida,Hippa_pacifica),((Aegla_platensis,(Lomis_hirta,Kiwa_hirsuta,Uroptychus_nitidus)),(Munida_gregaria,Galathea_strigosa,Pleuroncodes_planipes,(Petrolisthes_cinctipes,Petrolisthes_armatus,Porcellana_platycheles,Euceramus_praelongus)),((Dardanus_venosus,Clibanarius_vittatus,(Coenobita_clypeatus,Birgus_latro)),(Pagurus_bernhardus,Pagurus_longicarpus,(Paralithodes_camtschaticus,Paralithodes_platypus,Lithodes_maja)))))));")

# 1 = crab-like, 0 = not crab-like
crab_like <- c(
  # Outgroups: lobster and crayfish
  Homarus_americanus = 0,          # American lobster
  Procambarus_clarkii = 0,         # red swamp crayfish
  # True crabs (Brachyura)
  Dromia_personata = 1,            # sponge crab (wears a sponge as a hat)
  Homola_barbata = 0,              # carrier crab (tucked abdomen but narrow shell)
  Ranina_ranina = 0,               # frog crab / spanner crab
  Callinectes_sapidus = 1,         # Atlantic blue crab
  Cancer_pagurus = 1,              # edible crab
  Macrocheira_kaempferi = 1,       # Japanese spider crab (legs up to ~4 m across!)
  Carcinus_maenas = 1,             # European green crab
  Menippe_mercenaria = 1,          # Florida stone crab
  Ocypode_quadrata = 1,            # Atlantic ghost crab
  Leptuca_pugilator = 1,           # sand fiddler crab
  Grapsus_grapsus = 1,             # Sally Lightfoot crab
  # False crabs (Anomura)
  Emerita_analoga = 0,             # Pacific mole crab / sand crab
  Emerita_talpoida = 0,            # Atlantic mole crab
  Hippa_pacifica = 0,              # mole crab
  Aegla_platensis = 0,             # freshwater squat lobster
  Lomis_hirta = 1,                 # hairy stone crab (only found in southern Australia)
  Kiwa_hirsuta = 0,                # yeti crab (hairy, lives on deep-sea vents)
  Uroptychus_nitidus = 0,          # deep-sea squat lobster
  Munida_gregaria = 0,             # Patagonian squat lobster
  Galathea_strigosa = 0,           # spiny squat lobster
  Pleuroncodes_planipes = 0,       # "tuna crab" (actually a squat lobster)
  Petrolisthes_cinctipes = 1,      # flat porcelain crab
  Petrolisthes_armatus = 1,        # green porcelain crab
  Porcellana_platycheles = 1,      # broad-clawed porcelain crab
  Euceramus_praelongus = 0,        # olivepit porcelain crab (long and skinny)
  Dardanus_venosus = 0,            # star-eye hermit crab
  Clibanarius_vittatus = 0,        # thinstripe hermit crab
  Coenobita_clypeatus = 0,         # Caribbean land hermit crab (the pet store one)
  Birgus_latro = 0,                # coconut crab (a giant hermit crab that ditched the shell)
  Pagurus_bernhardus = 0,          # common hermit crab
  Pagurus_longicarpus = 0,         # long-wristed hermit crab
  Paralithodes_camtschaticus = 1,  # red king crab
  Paralithodes_platypus = 1,       # blue king crab
  Lithodes_maja = 1                # Norway king crab
)
```

2. Our ASR methods need every node to split in two, so we'll randomly resolve the polytomies with `multi2di()`. We don't have real branch lengths for this tree (it was assembled from several studies), so we'll set every branch to length 1.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
tr <- multi2di(decapods)
tr <- compute.brlen(tr, 1)

body <- setNames(ifelse(crab_like[tr$tip.label] == 1, "crab", "not_crab"), tr$tip.label)
cols <- c(crab = "orangered", not_crab = "steelblue")

plot(tr, cex = 0.7, label.offset = 0.1, tip.color = cols[body])
legend("topleft", legend = c("crab-like", "not crab-like"), fill = cols, bty = "n")
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 1 - 2

- **Make a prediction before you run anything.** Just by looking at the tree and the colors, how many times do you think the crab body evolved? Was the common ancestor of all crabs (true and false) crab-like?
- King crabs look like true crabs. Where are they on the tree, and who are their closest relatives? Does that surprise you?
```

### Method 1: Parsimony

3. **Parsimony** asks: what is the *smallest* number of changes (gains or losses of the crab body) needed to explain the colors on the tips?

```{r, eval=FALSE}
body_data <- phyDat(as.matrix(body), type = "USER", levels = c("crab", "not_crab"))
parsimony(tr, body_data)
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Question 3

- What is the minimum number of changes? Draw (or describe) one scenario on the tree that uses exactly that number of changes. How many are gains and how many are losses in your scenario?
```

### Method 2: Maximum likelihood

4. Parsimony gives one answer and no measure of uncertainty. **Maximum likelihood** fits a model where the trait can switch between states at some rate, and gives the **probability** that each ancestor was crab-like:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
fit <- ace(body, tr, type = "discrete", model = "ER")

plot(tr, cex = 0.7, label.offset = 0.1, tip.color = cols[body])
nodelabels(pie = fit$lik.anc, piecol = cols, cex = 0.5)
legend("topleft", legend = c("crab-like", "not crab-like"), fill = cols, bty = "n")
```

Each pie chart is an ancestor. The more orange the pie, the more likely that ancestor was crab-like.

5. Let's get the exact probabilities for some important ancestors. `getMRCA()` finds the most recent common ancestor of two species:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
anc <- fit$lik.anc
rownames(anc) <- (Ntip(tr) + 1):(Ntip(tr) + tr$Nnode)

prob_crab <- function(sp1, sp2) {
  round(anc[as.character(getMRCA(tr, c(sp1, sp2))), "crab"], 2)
}

prob_crab("Dromia_personata", "Lithodes_maja")        # ancestor of ALL crabs (true + false)
prob_crab("Emerita_analoga", "Lithodes_maja")         # ancestor of false crabs (Anomura)
prob_crab("Dromia_personata", "Ocypode_quadrata")     # ancestor of true crabs (Brachyura)
prob_crab("Pagurus_bernhardus", "Lithodes_maja")      # ancestor of hermit crabs + king crabs
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Questions 4 - 5

- Was the ancestor of the false crabs (Anomura) crab-like? Was the ancestor of the true crabs (Brachyura)? How confident is each answer? Based on this, how many times did the crab body evolve *within* the true crabs?
- King crabs are crab-like. Their ancestor with hermit crabs was not. So what was the ancestor of king crabs carrying around on its back?
```

### Method 3: Counting gains and losses

6. **Stochastic character mapping** simulates 100 possible histories of the trait on the tree, in proportion to how likely each one is. Then we can count how many gains and losses happen in an average history:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
maps <- make.simmap(tr, body, model = "ER", nsim = 100, message = FALSE)
history <- summary(maps)

colMeans(history$count)   # N = total changes; then crab -> not_crab (losses), not_crab -> crab (gains)
plot(history, colors = cols, fsize = 0.6)
```

```{block, type='rmdquestion'}
### Question 6

- On average, how many times was the crab body **gained** and how many times was it **lost**? Why is the total higher than the parsimony number from Question 3?
```
